summary: Specifies a per-domain technique for establishing inter-domain TE label switched paths, where each domain computes its own part of the path. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic engineering path can cross several networks that do not tell each other what their internal layout looks like. This RFC works around that: the setup signal moves forward one network at a time, and each network decides how the path runs through its own part before handing the signal on.

questions: what is an inter-domain te lsp
what is ero expansion in rsvp-te
subtitle: Let each domain work out its own stretch of a long MPLS or GMPLS path as the setup signal moves along.

tldr.problem: The head-end router of a traffic engineering path often cannot see a complete path across several areas or autonomous systems, so it cannot compute the whole route itself.
tldr.mechanism: The signaling message names the destination and the next boundary routers. Each boundary router computes the path through its own domain and passes the setup on, using crankback to try another exit when a domain fails.
tldr.outcome: Inter-domain TE LSPs can be set up without sharing topology between domains, but the result is not guaranteed to be optimal or to allow diverse paths.

facts.value: T1 from R0 in AS1 to R6 in AS3

today: RFC 5152 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. It is one of several documents on inter-domain traffic engineering, and it defines the path computation procedures that go with the signaling mechanism of RFC 5151.

sections.title: Why the Path Is Computed Piece by Piece
sections.content:
The requirements for inter-domain traffic engineering, both inter-area and inter-AS, were developed by the Traffic Engineering Working Group and stated in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216. The framework for inter-domain MPLS traffic engineering was provided in RFC 4726, and some of the mechanisms used to establish and maintain inter-domain TE LSPs are specified in RFC 5151 and RFC 5150.

This document focuses on the path computation aspects and defines a method for establishing inter-domain TE LSPs in which each node in charge of computing a section of the path is always along the path of that TE LSP. When the visibility of a complete end-to-end path spanning multiple domains is not available at the head-end LSR, the approach is a per-domain path computation during LSP setup, which determines the inter-domain TE LSP as it traverses multiple domains.

The mechanisms are equally applicable to MPLS TE domains other than IGP areas and autonomous systems. The solution does not attempt to address all the requirements of RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, which is acceptable because a solution may be developed for a particular deployment scenario. The technique is also one among many: the choice must be driven by the requirements for path attributes and by the deployment scenario. If the requirement is an end-to-end constraint-based shortest path across multiple domains, a mechanism using one or more distributed Path Computation Elements could be used instead, as described in RFC 4655. A service provider may also use different inter-domain path computation techniques for different TE LSP types.
sections.plainLanguage: There are other ways to do this, such as giving the job to a central controller that can see everything. This RFC takes the opposite approach: no one sees the whole path, so each network works out its own section.

sections.title: What the Method Assumes
sections.content:
Each domain in the examples is assumed to be capable of doing traffic engineering, running OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE together with RSVP-TE. A domain may itself comprise several other domains, for example an AS made of several sub-ASs in a BGP confederation or several areas or levels, in which case the technique applies recursively. The inter-domain TE LSPs are signaled using RSVP-TE.

The path, specified by an ERO in an RSVP-TE Path message, may be signaled as a set of loose and/or strict hops. The hops may identify the complete strict path end to end across different domains, the complete strict path in the source domain followed by boundary LSRs or domain identifiers such as AS numbers, the complete list of boundary LSRs along the path, or the current boundary LSR and the LSP destination. The set of hops can be statically configured on the head-end LSR or dynamically computed. The method defines an optional auto-discovery mechanism, based on IGP, BGP or policy routing information, that yields the next-hop boundary node, the domain exit point such as an ABR or ASBR, as the TE LSP is signaled, along with potential crankback mechanisms. The domain exit points may also be statically configured, in which case auto-discovery is not required.

Boundary LSRs are assumed to be capable of local path computation to expand a loose next hop when the path is not signaled as a set of strict hops, or when the strict hop is an abstract node such as an AS. In any case no topology or resource information needs to be distributed between domains, which is critical to preserve IGP and BGP scalability and confidentiality for TE LSPs spanning multiple routing domains.

Paths for the intra-domain hierarchical LSP or stitched LSP, or for a contiguous TE LSP within the domain, may be pre-configured or computed dynamically from the arriving inter-domain setup request, depending on the requirements of the transit domain. While some constraints such as bandwidth can be used across different domains, others such as resource affinity, color and metric may need to be translated at domain boundaries, and a local mapping based on policy agreement is assumed to exist where required.
sections.plainLanguage: The method needs three things: every network runs traffic engineering of its own, the setup signal is RSVP-TE, and each border router is able to work out a route inside its own network on demand. No network has to tell any other network what its internal map looks like.

sections.title: The Computation Procedure
sections.content:
The mechanisms work whether the inter-domain TE LSP is contiguous, stitched or nested. When a boundary node such as an ABR or ASBR receives a Path message whose ERO contains a strict node, the procedures of RFC 3209 apply and no further action is needed. When it receives an ERO with a loose hop, or an abstract node that identifies more than one LSR, it MUST follow the procedures of RFC 5151.

The first step is to find the next hop. If the next hop is not present in the Traffic Engineering Database, the LSR MUST check whether the IP address of the next-hop boundary LSR is outside the current domain and whether the next-hop domain is packet switch capable and uses an in-band control channel. If both conditions hold, the boundary LSR SHOULD check whether the next hop has IP reachability via IGP or BGP. If it does not, a signaling failure occurs and the LSR SHOULD send back an RSVP PathErr message with error code 24, Routing Problem. If the routing information indicates the next hop is reachable, the selected route is expected to pass through a domain boundary via a boundary LSR, and this determination is what the document calls auto-discovery. Without such a mechanism, the ABR or ASBR in the next-hop domain must be the signaled loose next hop in the ERO, or some other scheme must provide the domain exit points. An implementation MAY instead support disabling the IP reachability fallback so that a missing next hop always triggers a signaling failure.

Once the next-hop boundary LSR is known, a contiguous TE LSP is handled by having the boundary LSR perform an ERO expansion, which computes the constrained path up to the next loose hop and adds the list of hops as strict nodes in the ERO, unless policy forbids it. If no path satisfying the constraints can be found, that is treated as a path computation and signaling failure, and an RSVP PathErr message SHOULD be sent.

For a stitched or nested TE LSP, if the boundary LSR is a candidate for intra-area H-LSP or S-LSP setup and the TE LSP is a candidate for hierarchy or nesting, and if there is no H-LSP or S-LSP from this LSR to the next-hop boundary LSR that satisfies the constraints, it SHOULD signal one. A pre-configured H-LSP or S-LSP may be selected instead, and local policy MAY allow a new one to be signaled if that selection fails. If the boundary LSR is not a candidate for nesting or stitching, or the TE LSP is not a candidate for hierarchy, the same procedure as the contiguous case applies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each border router does the same three things: work out which border router in the next network to send the signal to, find a route inside its own network that meets the requested constraints, and pass the signal on. If it cannot find such a route, it reports a failure upstream.

sections.title: A Walk Through an Inter-Area Path
sections.content:
The example topology has three areas. ABR1, ABR2, ABR3 and ABR4 are area border routers, X1 is an LSR in area 1, X2 and X3 are LSRs in area 2, and an inter-area TE LSP T0 is originated at R0 in area 1 and terminated at R1 in area 2. The terminology follows OSPF, but the technique applies equally to an IS-IS multi-level network.

For a contiguous TE LSP, the head-end LSR R0 first determines the next-hop ABR, either configured by the user or found by the auto-discovery mechanism. R0 computes the path to reach that ABR and signals the Path message. When the message reaches ABR1, it determines the next-hop ABR from its own area, say ABR3, either directly from the ERO when the next-hop ABR is a loose hop or by auto-discovery. The hops might be a set of loose hops, for example R0-ABR1(loose)-ABR3(loose)-R1(loose), or a mix of strict and loose hops, for example R0-X1-ABR1-ABR3(loose)-X2-X3-R1.

A set of paths can be configured on the head-end LSR ordered by priority, each with its own constraints. A last-resort option with no constraint can make sure the LSP can always be set up if at least a TE path exists, and an implementation might retry a particular path option a configurable number of times before trying a lower-priority one.

Once ABR1 has computed the path up to ABR3, it sends the Path message along it. ABR3 repeats the procedure. If ABR3 cannot find a path obeying the constraints, signaling stops and ABR3 sends a PathErr to ABR1. ABR1 can then trigger a new path computation by selecting another egress boundary LSR, ABR4 in the example, if crankback is allowed for this inter-area TE LSP. If crankback is not allowed, or ABR1 is configured not to perform it, ABR1 MUST stop signaling and forward the PathErr up to the head-end LSR R0 without trying another ABR.
sections.plainLanguage: Walking through the example: the router that starts the path picks a border router to aim at, the border router picks the next one and computes its own stretch, and the setup rolls forward in that way. If a stretch fails, the error travels back and the previous router may try a different exit if policy allows.

sections.title: Optimality and the Trapping Problem
sections.content:
Because the inter-domain TE LSP is computed on a per-domain basis, the optimal inter-domain path cannot be guaranteed. Computing two diverse paths with a per-domain approach may also not be possible in some topologies, because of the trapping problem.

The example topology has four routers, A, B, C and D, with A-B and B-C on the upper path and A and D joined by a lower path. With a serialized approach using the per-domain technique, a first TE LSP may be computed along A-B-C-D, after which no diverse path can be found, even though two diverse paths exist: A-C-D and A-B-D. The point of the example is that a per-domain approach may fail to find diverse paths that do exist.

The required path computation method can be selected by the service provider on a per-LSP basis. If the per-domain technique does not meet the requirements for a particular TE LSP, such as path optimality or the need for a set of diversely routed LSPs, other techniques such as PCE-based path computation may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Because each network picks its own route, the result is not always the best possible one, and sometimes two routes that do not share any link cannot be found even when they exist. Providers that need those guarantees should use a different method.

sections.title: Reoptimizing an Established Path
sections.content:
The ability to reoptimize an already established inter-domain TE LSP is a requirement, and the process differs with the nature of the LSP and the mechanism used to compute it.

For a contiguous TE LSP, a better route may appear inside any traversed domain after setup, and it is desirable to reroute the LSP in a non-disruptive fashion using the Make-Before-Break procedure. RFC 4736 proposes a mechanism that notifies the head-end LSR of a more optimal path in a downstream domain, and the head-end LSR may then decide to reroute gracefully. For a contiguous LSP the reoptimization is strictly controlled by the head-end LSR, regardless of where the better path is.

For a stitched or nested inter-domain TE LSP, reoptimization is a local matter for each domain, because the inter-domain TE LSP is a different LSP, and a different RSVP session, from the intra-domain S-LSP or H-LSP in an area or AS. Reoptimization in a domain is done by locally reoptimizing the intra-domain H-LSP or S-LSP, and since the inter-domain TE LSPs are transported over these, reoptimizing them reoptimizes the inter-domain paths. No additional RSVP signaling is required, and reoptimization is transparent to the head-end LSR. Reoptimization parameters such as frequency and criteria can vary from one domain to another. If the operator does not want local reoptimization, the procedures of RFC 4736 MUST be used, and any reoptimization event within the domain MUST be reported to the head-end node.

An operator may still trigger reoptimization manually at the head-end LSR. That trigger SHOULD force a reoptimization by signaling a new path for the same LSP using Make-Before-Break; the boundary LSR then initiates a new S-LSP setup or selects an existing or new H-LSP, and once setup along the new path is complete the head-end LSR switches the traffic over and the old path is eventually torn down. The head-end LSR does not know in advance whether a more optimal path exists, and such a manual trigger is not considered a frequent occurrence.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the path is up, a better route may appear inside one of the networks. For a path built in one piece, the router that started it decides when to move. For a path stitched from per-network pieces, each network improves its own piece on its own schedule, and the change is invisible to the router that started the path.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Signaling inter-domain TE LSPs raises security issues, which are discussed in Section 7 of RFC 5151. RFC 4726 provides an overview of the requirements for security in an MPLS-TE or GMPLS multi-domain environment. When signaling an inter-domain RSVP-TE LSP, an operator may use the security features already defined for RSVP-TE, which may require coordination between the domains to share keys and care to ensure that the keys are changed sufficiently frequently. This may involve extra synchronization when domain border nodes are protected with Fast Reroute, since the merge point and the point of local repair should also share the key.

For an inter-domain TE LSP, especially one that traverses different administrative or trust domains, the RFC says three mechanisms SHOULD be available to an operator: a way to enforce policies and filters at domain borders when processing incoming setup requests, based on agreed trust and service levels between domains, with attributes such as bandwidth and priority as part of the contract; a way to rate-limit LSP setup requests or error notifications from a particular domain; and a mechanism for policy-based outbound RSVP message processing at the domain border node, which may involve filtering or modifying certain addresses in RSVP objects and messages.

The document notes that the process for establishing paths does not increase the information exchanged between ASs and preserves topology confidentiality. That said, signaling an inter-domain TE LSP requires path computation on boundary nodes that may be exposed to various attacks, so it is RECOMMENDED to support policy decisions that reject the ERO expansion of an inter-domain TE LSP when it is not allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the setup signal crosses administrative borders, the RFC asks for rate limiting, filtering and agreed policies at those borders, and for a way to refuse a path expansion that policy does not permit. It also notes that the method does not reveal more of each network's map than before.
